$comment: Root index of contract families. A family exists here or it does not exist. validate_contracts.py checks this in both directions: every directory has a row, every row has a directory.

families.name: common
families.description: Shapes referenced across families. Adding one here rather than duplicating it is what keeps two families from drifting on the same concept.

families.name: endpoints
families.description: Model B endpoint addressing: the routing selector beneath a PeerId, its configuration, direct destinations, the delivered event, and the endpoint-directory reply.

families.name: ipc
families.description: The local IPC v2 boundary: handshake and endpoint claim, capability grants, the message-class frame body, and the directed-send parameters whose deliberate omission of a source endpoint is what makes the source non-spoofable.

families.name: direct
families.description: The directed-messaging vocabulary that is genuinely document-shaped: the coarse rejection codes a remote peer may see, how a sender addressed the message, and the deduplication key. The DirectMessageV2 byte framing is deliberately not modelled here — see the family manifest's not_modelled note.

families.name: identity
families.description: The offline recovery record: 24 words plus the public metadata that proves a restore reconstructed the intended identity. A bearer secret that never crosses IPC, Channel, or the network — schematised so a backup file can be validated offline, not because it is ever transmitted.

families.name: discovery
families.description: Advisory reachability observations and the providers that emit them. Candidates grant nothing: EndpointIds, channels, roles, and presence are explicitly outside discovery, and the closed candidate shape is what keeps them out.

families.name: connectivity
families.description: The backend-neutral view of Internet reachability — normalized states and counts, deliberately without the infrastructure identities behind them.

families.name: human-chat
families.description: The first-party human message envelope. An APPLICATION protocol above the payload-agnostic transport, versioning independently of it.

not_modelled.gossipsub: There is no `gossipsub` family, and that is a decision rather than a gap. Broadcast's one wire document is the `BroadcastMessageV1` envelope, which is a fixed-width binary layout JSON Schema cannot express — the same boundary DIRECT.md draws for `DirectMessageV2`, and it is frozen the same way, as byte vectors in `fixtures/gossipsub/broadcast-message-v1-frame.json`. Its other externally visible values are derived rather than transmitted: the topic key and `GossipSubMessageIdV1` are hashes, frozen in `fixtures/gossipsub/` beside it. The vocabulary broadcast does share with the rest of the transport is already modelled where it belongs — `common/channel-id` names the channel, and ADR-0030 keeps EndpointId out of broadcast entirely, so there is no endpoint-shaped document to describe. A local delivery shape for broadcast is not modelled either: like direct's, it is an in-process event until an IPC surface carries it.
not_modelled.kademlia: There is no `kademlia` family, and that is a decision rather than a gap. ADR-0049 schematises WIRE shapes — documents that cross a boundary as JSON — and Kademlia has none. The control surface in `crates/api/kademlia-control-api` is an in-process port between the provider and the Swarm-owned driver: it never crosses IPC or the network. Kademlia's peer observations reach consumers as ordinary `discovery.candidate-peer` documents, which ARE modelled. Its one externally visible string, the `/interweave/kad/1.0.0/<network-hash>` protocol name, is a derived value rather than a document and is frozen in `fixtures/kademlia/kad-network-namespace-v1.json`. And the DHT stores nothing: record mode is disabled (ADR-0009), so there is no record shape to describe. A `kademlia` family would therefore have to invent documents nothing transmits.
